name: Sam Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union or party, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five and at the depot on the ring road by quarter past six to load the van. It's my own van, a white 2014 Transit with 190,000 on the clock, and I do parcels for Rushly, which is an app that pays me per drop. On a good day that's 140 drops across the estates and the old town, and on a Friday night I sometimes do takeaway runs on the same app to top up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being on my own in the cab with the radio, and I know every cut-through and every dog on my route. What wears me out is the app changing the rate without asking anyone. Last spring they dropped the price per drop from £1.20 to £1.05 and there was nobody to complain to, just a chat bot that kept saying sorry for the inconvenience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that the problem was never the robots, it's the people who own the app. Even if AI does nothing, Rushly, the parcel app I drive for, will still find a way to cut the rate per drop. I'd put that in the drivers' group chat for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes, and nothing changing is bad enough. Lucia and I have maybe three weeks of money in the bank, and the van needs new tyres before winter. One bad month, a broken clutch, and we're behind on rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the route, same as now, because there isn't really another depot within an hour of us. I'd try to put £20 a week in a jar for the van, which sounds tiny but it's what I can do. And I'd go along to the meeting about a couriers' union that a lad from the depot keeps on about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, more than scared. It's the same knot in my stomach I've had since I started, it's just not getting any looser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the van. If it broke down tomorrow, what would happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't earn, simple as that, because Rushly doesn't care whose van it is. Last time the alternator went I lost four days and borrowed £300 off my brother Diego, which I'm still paying back. I hated asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the lad who's setting up the union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm in, but I'm not standing at the front. If Rushly sees your face on a poster, your route somehow gets the far estates and the flats with no lifts. I've seen it happen to Marek, who stood up at the depot last year.

say: The real problem is **the app owners**, not the robots, and I'd say so in the drivers' group chat.
Even with no big AI change, Rushly will still find a way to **cut the rate**.
think: Nothing changing is still bad, because we only have about **three weeks** of money saved.
One **broken clutch** or a month of low drops puts us behind on rent.
do: Keep running the same **parcel route** because there's no other depot within an hour.
Put **£20 a week** in a jar for van repairs and new tyres before winter.
Go to the **couriers' union** meeting, but stay out of sight at the back.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, with the same knot in his stomach he's had for years.
S0.quote: Even if AI does nothing, Rushly, the parcel app I drive for, will still find a way to cut the rate per drop.
fieldNote: Sam's worry is **already here**: a rate cut last spring, thin savings and a 2014 van.
He backs a union in principle but fears being **singled out**, after what happened to a colleague, Marek.
He frames everything as **owners versus drivers**; technology itself barely registers for him.

steps.text: Keep doing the Rushly parcel route from the ring-road depot
Put £20 a week in a jar for van tyres and repairs
Attend the couriers' union meeting a depot colleague is organising

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the office people, because now they'll find out what we've lived with for years. The app already plans my route and talks to the customers for me. I'd probably say online that if your boss is software, you need a union even more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What scares me is all those office people losing work and signing up to Rushly. More drivers means fewer drops each, and the app will drop the rate again because it can. My job isn't going to a robot soon, it's going to a laid-off bank clerk with a hatchback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly, pay the subs, which I think is about £8 a month. I'd stop the Friday takeaway runs in the van because the diesel barely covers it, and I'd ask Lucia if her care home needs drivers for the minibus. I'm not going to learn computers, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Squeezed. Like the van's already full and someone keeps throwing more boxes in the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn computers. What if Rushly makes you use a new AI system to scan and route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'll use whatever button they make me press, same as I do now. But I won't go home and play with chat bots. I've got my phone for the app and for calling my mum, and that's enough screen for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home if the drops go down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, which I barely use anyway, and the takeaways ourselves, which is funny given what I do. Then the phone contract goes down to a cheaper one. Rent and the van insurance are the two I'd never miss.

say: Office workers will now find out what **app drivers** have lived with for years.
If your boss is **software**, you need a union even more than before.
think: The real threat is **laid-off office workers** signing up to deliver and splitting the drops.
More drivers means Rushly will **cut the rate** again, simply because it can.
do: Join the union properly and pay the **£8 a month** subs.
Stop the **Friday takeaway runs** because diesel eats most of the money.
Ask about driving the **care-home minibus** where his partner Lucia works.
feel: **Squeezed**, as if the van is full and more boxes keep coming.
S1.quote: My job isn't going to a robot soon, it's going to a laid-off bank clerk with a hatchback.
fieldNote: Sam sees the threat as **more competition** for drops, not robots, which is sharp for a hands-on job.
He firmly **refuses to learn AI** tools, though he'll press whatever the app makes him press.
His fallback idea is a **minibus job** through his partner's workplace, showing how few local options he has.

steps.text: Join the couriers' union and pay the £8 monthly subs
Drop the Friday takeaway runs that barely cover the diesel
Ask Lucia's care home about a minibus driving job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting about it, honestly, saying the government needs to protect people before the robots turn up. I'd say there should be a tax on these companies and money for drivers who get pushed out. I'd share every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think anyone's going to save me. By 2028 the thinking bit is gone, and the app's already the thinking bit, so it'll just get tighter. Then by 2031 there's a robot van, and I'll be 32 with no qualifications and a route nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd do my HGV licence if I could find the money, because lorries feel like they'd last a bit longer. That's about £3,000, which I don't have, so maybe the union or the council would help. Once it arrives I'd be at every protest, and I'd probably have to move to Lucia's parents' place to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like when you see the blue lights in the mirror and you don't know yet what you did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said lorries might last longer. Why lorries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a lorry has to back into some farm yard with a gate that sticks, and I can't see a robot doing that by 2031. That's just a guess, though. I don't actually know, nobody at the depot knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we might have to move in with her mum and dad for a year, and she'd hate that. Her dad thinks I should have joined the army. It'd be a long, quiet dinner.

say: The **government** must protect drivers before the robot vans arrive.
There should be a **tax on the companies** and support for drivers pushed out.
think: He doesn't believe **anyone will save** him, and the app will only get tighter.
By about 2031 he'll be **32 with no qualifications** and a route nobody needs.
do: Try to fund an **HGV licence**, about £3,000, through the union or council.
Join **protests and petitions** once AGI arrives.
Move in with his partner's **parents** to save on rent.
feel: **Sick** and dreading something he can't yet see clearly.
**Powerless**, because he doesn't think public promises will reach drivers like him.
S2.quote: By 2031 there's a robot van, and I'll be 32 with no qualifications and a route nobody needs.
fieldNote: The **three-year robot gap** matters to Sam: he plans to use it for an HGV licence.
His public line asks for **state help**; privately he expects none to arrive in time.
Moving in with his partner's parents is a real cost to his **pride**, and he says so.

steps.text: Apply for union or council help to pay for an HGV licence
Join drivers' protests and sign petitions for a company tax
Move in with Lucia's parents for a year to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as with the fast one, but I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government to sit on its hands. I'd be on at the union to push for a deal for drivers now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's enough time to get the HGV licence slowly and maybe some years of lorry work. But I'm not stupid. Five years for the AI and eight for the robots, so around 2034 I'm 35 and the lorries go too, just a bit later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the HGV licence in the first year, paying it off a bit at a time, maybe £150 a month. I'd keep doing Rushly while I train because there's nothing else to pay the rent. And I'd go to the union's meetings every month instead of hiding at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but it's more like a deadline than a cliff. I can work with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop hiding at the back. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there's five years, then everyone's in the same boat and Rushly can't punish all of us. In the fast one, it's every man for himself. With time, people actually turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the £150 a month come from, with three weeks saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I can't answer properly. Probably more Saturday shifts and no holiday for two years. Lucia wanted to go to her cousin's wedding in the summer, and that might have to go.

say: With **five years** of warning, the government has no excuse to sit on its hands.
The union should push for a **deal for drivers** now, not after AGI lands.
think: By around **2034**, age 35, he expects robot vans to reach his route.
An **HGV licence** buys some years, but he knows lorries will go later too.
do: Start the **HGV licence** in year one, paying about £150 a month.
Keep driving for **Rushly** while training to cover rent.
Attend **union meetings** monthly and speak up instead of hiding.
feel: Worried, but it feels like a **deadline** rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: Five years for the AI and eight for the robots, so around 2034 I'm 35 and the lorries go too, just a bit later.
fieldNote: More warning makes Sam **braver**: he would speak up at union meetings rather than hide.
He can't say where the **£150 a month** comes from; he'd skip holidays and work Saturdays.
He still expects to lose driving work entirely, so the extra time **delays** rather than removes his fear.

steps.text: Start HGV licence training, paying about £150 a month
Keep driving the Rushly route while training
Speak up at the union's monthly drivers' meeting
Skip the summer trip to Lucia's cousin's wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, with retraining that's actually paid for and not some online course. I'd say it at the depot and I'd probably vote for whoever promised that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for the AI and thirteen for the robots, so I'd be 40 before a robot takes my seat in the van. That's a whole career in lorries, or something else. I'm less scared of this one, but I don't trust that I'll use the time well, because I'm not good at change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the HGV licence over two years, no rush, and try to get a proper job at a haulage firm with a contract and sick pay. I'd keep paying the union. I'd vote for the party that talks about retraining money, which is who I'd vote for anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, to be honest. Ten years sounds like forever when you're 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at change. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, mainly. I'd tell myself I'll start next year, and then it's 2032. Lucia would have to push me, she's the one who books everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, who's 58 and has done parcels for 20 years. He'd be 68 when the robots come, so maybe he's fine, but he's got nothing saved either. He eats his lunch in the van every day, same sandwich.

say: Ten years is enough for **paid retraining**, not just an online course.
He'd **vote** for whoever promises real retraining money for drivers.
think: He'd be **40** before a robot takes his seat, so there's time for a lorry career.
His real fear is himself: he's **not good at change** and might waste the decade.
do: Take the **HGV licence** over two years without rushing it.
Look for a **haulage job** with a contract and sick pay.
Keep paying **union subs** and vote for retraining money.
feel: **Calmer**, because ten years feels like forever at 27.
A little **ashamed** that he might put off starting.
S4.quote: Ten years for the AI and thirteen for the robots, so I'd be 40 before a robot takes my seat in the van.
fieldNote: Sam's mood **eases** with a decade, but thin savings and a 2014 van keep him anxious.
He names his own **procrastination** as the main risk and relies on his partner, Lucia, to push him.
His concern for an older colleague, Ray, shows he thinks about the **depot as a group**.

steps.text: Take the HGV licence over two years
Apply to haulage firms offering contracts and sick pay
Vote for the party promising paid retraining for drivers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and no money to change anything. What would help is someone paying for the HGV licence and a union that Rushly actually has to talk to. A real person to ring when the rate drops would be a start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money when the robots do the driving. When the robots do the driving, the money won't go to Ray, the oldest driver at my depot, and it won't go to me. That's the bit that actually makes me angry.

headlineQuote: When the robots do the driving, the money won't go to Ray, the oldest driver at my depot, and it won't go to me.
portrait: Sam is **27**, drives his own 2014 van for a parcel app and lives with his partner, Lucia.
He has about **three weeks** of savings and already feels squeezed by app rate cuts.
He blames **platform owners**, backs unions and refuses to use AI tools himself.
Faster AGI pushes him from anxious to **alarmed**; his plan in every case is an HGV licence.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because he'd have no time or money to change.
whatWouldHelp: Someone paying for his **HGV licence**, and a union Rushly must negotiate with.
